name: Shadoof
desc: The shadoof is a tool for lifting water from a well, river or pond onto land or into a channel: a long pole pivoted on an upright frame, with a bucket at one end and a counterweight of clay or stone at the other. The earliest evidence of it is a cylinder seal from Mesopotamia of about 2200 BCE; it appeared in Upper Egypt sometime after 2000 BCE and reached China around the same time. One man can lift 39 to 130 litres a minute with it, and it is still used for irrigation in Africa, Asia and parts of Europe.

name: Noria
desc: A noria is a water wheel turned by a river's current whose rim carries pots, buckets or compartments that lift water into a small aqueduct, for irrigation or to supply towns. Paddle-driven water-lifting wheels had appeared in Egypt by the 4th century BCE; the Roman architect Vitruvius described the noria in the 1st century BCE, and around 300 CE the Romans tied ceramic pots to an open-framed wheel. Muslim engineers adopted and improved it: Ibn Bassal of al-Andalus fitted a flywheel, and Ismail al-Jazari a crank in 1206. The norias of Hama in Syria were 20 metres across.

name: Canning
desc: Canning is a method of preserving food by processing it and sealing it in an airtight container, a glass jar or a steel or tin can. In 1809 the French confectioner and brewer Nicolas Appert, answering a government prize of 12,000 francs for preserved rations for the Grande Armée, developed a way of sealing food in glass jars, and was awarded the prize in 1810. In London Peter Durand patented the tin can process in 1810, and Bryan Donkin made sealed cans of tinned wrought iron, sold chiefly to the British Army and Royal Navy. Why the food kept was explained only when Louis Pasteur showed the role of microbes.

name: Mechanical reaper
desc: A mechanical reaper is a machine that cuts, and often gathers, grain crops at harvest. Patrick Bell built one in Scotland in 1828; in the United States Obed Hussey patented a reaper in 1833 and Cyrus McCormick a horse-drawn one in 1834, completing a design begun by his father Robert, with the aid of Jo Anderson, a man enslaved by the family. Reapers spread slowly until McCormick acquired the rights to Hussey's cutter bar around 1850. The reaper-binder of 1872 also bound the sheaves, and it was replaced in turn by the swather and the combine harvester.

name: Tractor
desc: A tractor is an engine-powered vehicle that pulls or drives farm machinery. The first tractors were steam ploughing engines, which followed the self-propelled traction engine Thomas Aveling made in 1859; in 1889 John Charter of Illinois built the first gasoline-powered tractors, and John Froelich built another in Iowa in 1892. Dan Albone's Ivel Agricultural Motor of 1901 was the first commercially successful light petrol tractor, and Henry Ford's mass-produced Fordson of 1917 held 77% of the US market by 1923. By 1935 nearly a million tractors were in use in the United States.

name: Barbed wire
desc: Barbed wire is steel fencing wire with sharp points set at intervals along its strands, used for cheap fences and, as a wire obstacle, in trench warfare. In France Leonce Eugene Grassin-Baledans proposed a fence of thin wire with bristling points in 1860, and Louis François Janin patented a double wire with diamond-shaped barbs in 1865. In the United States Lucien B. Smith of Kent, Ohio, received the first patent in 1867, and Joseph Glidden of DeKalb, Illinois, patented the modern form in 1874. It made fencing the western plains cheap, and the open range was closed amid the Fence Cutting Wars of the 1880s.

name: Aquaculture
desc: Aquaculture is the farming of fish, crustaceans, molluscs, algae and other aquatic organisms under controlled or semi-natural conditions. Oral tradition in China places the culture of the common carp around 2000–2100 BCE, but the earliest significant evidence is The Classic of Fish Culture, a monograph by Fan Li written around 475 BCE. Romans bred fish in ponds and farmed oysters before 100 CE, medieval monasteries took up their methods, and Hawaiians built ocean fishponds. By 1866 artificial fish hatcheries operated in Canada and the United States, and world output reached 130.9 million tonnes in 2022.

name: Wine
desc: Wine is an alcoholic drink made by fermenting grapes. The earliest known traces of it, from about 6000 BCE, were found near Tbilisi in Georgia; jars from Hajj Firuz in Iran, of about 5000 BCE, held wine sealed with pine resin, and the Areni-1 cave in Armenia holds the oldest known winery, with a press, vats and jars from about 4100 BCE. Phoenicians and Greeks spread wine around the Mediterranean, the Romans enlarged its trade, and it became part of Jewish and Christian ritual. In the 19th century phylloxera forced the replanting of almost every vine in Europe.

name: Cheese
desc: Cheese is a food made by curdling milk. It was probably first made by accident, when milk was stored in bladders made of ruminants' stomachs, whose rennet curdles it. The earliest direct evidence is holed clay sieves more than seven thousand years old, from Kujawy in Poland and the Dalmatian coast of Croatia, where residues suggest cheese. Sumerian cuneiform texts of the Third Dynasty of Ur record it, remains were found in an Egyptian tomb of about 2900 BCE, the first cheese factory opened in Switzerland in 1815, and Jesse Williams began assembly-line production in New York in 1851.

name: Coffee
desc: Coffee is a drink brewed from the roasted seeds of the coffee plant, which grows wild in Ethiopia. There is no confirmed evidence of it being drunk before the 15th century, when Sufis in Yemen used it to stay alert during night prayers; Abd al-Qadir al-Jaziri reported that Jamal-al-Din al-Dhabhani, mufti of Aden, first adopted it around 1454. It reached Mecca, Cairo and Damascus, and the first coffeehouse in Istanbul opened in 1554. Until the end of the 17th century the Yemeni port of Mocha was its only gateway; by 1788 Saint-Domingue supplied half the world's coffee, and by 1852 Brazil was the largest producer.

name: Kuk Swamp
desc: Kuk Swamp is an archaeological site in the Wahgi Valley of the Papua New Guinea highlands, at about 1,550 metres, some 12–13 kilometres northeast of Mount Hagen. Drainage ditches dug there from about 9,000 years ago, from major disposal channels to small field ditches, turned the swamp into grassland where taro was grown, and bananas and sugar cane were cultivated from 6,900–6,400 years ago. Studied by the Australian archaeologist Jack Golson, it was made a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2008 as one of the places where people developed agriculture independently. The Kawelka people live in the area today.

name: Norfolk four-course system
desc: The Norfolk four-course system is a method of crop rotation in which four crops follow one another over a four-year cycle: wheat, turnips, barley, and clover or ryegrass. Unlike the earlier three-field system, it has no fallow year. It was developed in the early 16th century in Waasland, in present-day northern Belgium, and popularised in the 18th century by the British agriculturist Charles Townshend. Its fodder crop, turnips, and its grazing crop, clover, allowed livestock to be kept year-round, and it was a key development in the British Agricultural Revolution.

name: Seismoscope
desc: A seismoscope is an instrument that shows that the ground has shaken, without the continuous record that a seismometer keeps. The earliest well-documented one was made in 132 CE by Zhang Heng of the Han dynasty in China and called Houfeng Didong Yi. According to the History of the Later Han Dynasty, it was a bronze vessel about 2 metres across, with eight dragon's heads that dropped a ball into a bronze toad to show the direction of a quake. Mercury and pendulum seismoscopes followed in 18th-century Europe, and the modern seismometer was developed in the 19th century.

name: Water clock
desc: A water clock, or clepsydra, measures time by the regulated flow of water into or out of a vessel. Its oldest documentation is the tomb inscription of the 16th-century BCE Egyptian court official Amenemhet, which names him as its inventor, and the oldest surviving one, from the reign of Amenhotep III (c. 1417–1379 BCE), was used at Karnak. Babylonian tablets record water clocks used for the night and day watches, and the oldest written reference in China dates to the 6th century BCE. Ctesibius and other Hellenistic engineers added feedback control, gearing and dials, and water clocks stayed in use until mechanical clocks replaced them in Europe around 1300.

name: Sundial
desc: A sundial tells the time of day from the apparent position of the Sun, usually by the shadow that a gnomon casts on a dial marked with hour-lines. The earliest sundials known from the archaeological record are shadow clocks of about 1500 BCE from ancient Egyptian and Babylonian astronomy. By 240 BCE Eratosthenes had used an obelisk and a water well to estimate the circumference of the world, and the Roman writer Vitruvius listed the dials known in his day in De architectura. Canonical sundials marked the liturgical hours of religious orders from the 7th to the 14th centuries, and Giovanni Padovani published a treatise on making sundials in 1570.

name: Armillary sphere
desc: An armillary sphere is a model of the sky made of rings that stand for the celestial equator, the ecliptic and other circles, centred on the Earth or the Sun. It was invented separately in ancient Greece and in China. Hipparchus credited Eratosthenes (276–194 BCE) with its invention, and Greek armillary spheres served as teaching tools in the 3rd century BCE. In China, Geng Shouchang introduced a fixed equatorial ring in 52 BCE, and Zhang Heng completed the sphere with horizon and meridian rings in 125 CE and turned it by water power. Islamic and medieval European astronomers took it up, and it remained the main instrument for finding celestial positions until the telescope.

name: Trigonometry
desc: Trigonometry is the branch of mathematics that relates the angles of triangles to the lengths of their sides. It emerged in the Hellenistic world in the 3rd century BCE, when Euclid and Archimedes proved theorems on chords equivalent to later trigonometric formulae, and in 140 BCE Hipparchus gave the first tables of chords. Ptolemy set out detailed tables in his Almagest in the 2nd century CE, and the modern definition of the sine is first attested in the Indian Surya Siddhanta. Persian mathematicians such as Abu al-Wafa used all six trigonometric functions by the 10th century, and Nasir al-Din al-Tusi treated trigonometry as a discipline apart from astronomy.

name: Barometer
desc: A barometer is an instrument that measures air pressure, from which changes in the weather can be forecast. Evangelista Torricelli is usually credited with inventing it in 1643, though the historian W. E. Knowles Middleton holds 1644, when Torricelli first reported his experiments, the more likely date. After a water-tube experiment by Gasparo Berti and Raffaello Magiotti, Torricelli argued that the weight of the atmosphere, not the pull of a vacuum, held up the liquid, and he used mercury so that a tube of only 80 cm was needed. In September 1648 Florin Perier carried a barometer up the Puy de Dôme for Blaise Pascal and found that the mercury stood lower at altitude.

name: Thermometer
desc: A thermometer measures temperature through a change in a sensor that is read against a scale. Philo of Byzantium in the 3rd century BCE and Hero of Alexandria described devices in which heated and cooled air moved water, and in the late 16th and early 17th centuries Galileo Galilei and Santorio Santorio built thermoscopes, which had no scale. The first instrument shown with a scale, and so a thermometer, was Santorio's of 1625; in 1629 Joseph Solomon Delmedigo described a sealed liquid-in-glass thermometer. Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit made a reliable mercury thermometer in 1714, and Anders Celsius proposed his scale in 1742.

name: Kite
desc: A kite is a tethered craft heavier than air whose wing surfaces react against the wind to give lift. It was first made in China, where kites of silk and bamboo, and of paper after its invention in the Han dynasty, served to measure distances, test the wind, lift men and signal in war; by 549 CE a kite carried a message for a rescue mission. Kites spread to India, where the fighter kite developed, and across Polynesia, but reached Europe late: Konrad Kyeser described dragon kites about 1400. Benjamin Franklin published an account of a kite experiment on lightning in 1752, and kites served the research of the Wright brothers toward the first airplane.

name: Lathe
desc: A lathe is a machine tool that turns a workpiece about an axis while tools cut, sand, drill or shape it into a form symmetrical about that axis. Clear evidence of turning comes from the 6th century BCE: fragments of a wooden bowl in an Etruscan tomb in northern Italy and two wooden dishes with turned rims from present-day Turkey. A painting in the tomb of Petosiris in 4th-century BCE Egypt is the first known picture of a lathe, and in China rotary lathes sharpened tools and weapons by about 400 BCE. Andrey Nartov built a lathe with a tool-carrying carriage and gears in 1718, and by the 1770s precision lathes with a slide-rest had become practical.

name: Screw
desc: A screw is a helically threaded fastener tightened or released by twisting its head, and one of the six classical simple machines. It was one of the last simple machines to be invented, first appearing in Mesopotamia in the Neo-Assyrian period (911–609 BCE) and later in Ancient Egypt and Greece, where Archytas of Tarentum described it. By the 1st century BCE wooden screws drove the presses that pressed olive oil and grape juice around the Mediterranean. Metal screws became common fasteners only from the 1760s, when Job and William Wyatt patented a screw machine, and Jesse Ramsden made the first satisfactory screw-cutting lathe in 1777.

name: Loom
desc: A loom is a device for weaving cloth and tapestry that holds the warp threads under tension while the weft threads are passed over and under them. The earliest evidence of a horizontal loom is a picture on a pottery dish from ancient Egypt dated to 4400 BCE, showing a frame loom with treadles that left the weaver's hands free to pass and beat the weft. The warp-weighted loom, whose warp is kept taut by hanging weights, may go back to the Neolithic. The drawloom for patterned silk is first confirmed by fabrics from the State of Chu of about 400 BCE; it sped up Chinese silk weaving and was introduced to Persia, India and Europe.

name: Sewing needle
desc: A sewing needle is a slender pointed tool with an eye at one end to carry thread through material. A needle of bird bone found in Denisova Cave and attributed to the Denisovans is estimated to be about 50,000 years old, and a bone needle from Potok Cave in Slovenia dates to the Aurignacian, 47,000 to 41,000 years ago. Bone and ivory needles come from Xiaogushan in Liaoning and from Kostenki in Russia, and Flinders Petrie found copper sewing needles at Naqada in Egypt dating from 4400 to 3000 BCE. Iron needles are known from the third century BCE, and needle-making began at Redditch in England in 1639.

name: Pencil
desc: A pencil is a writing or drawing implement with a solid core of pigment, usually graphite, in a protective casing. Around 1560 the Italian couple Simonio and Lyndiana Bernacotti made what are likely the first plans for a wood-encased pencil, from a hollowed stick of juniper. In 1565 a large deposit of pure, solid graphite, then thought to be a form of lead and called plumbago, was found at Seathwaite in Borrowdale, Cumbria, England, and its sticks were at first wrapped in string or sheepskin. The first attempt to make graphite sticks from powder was in Nuremberg in 1662, and in 1795 Nicolas-Jacques Conté fired powdered graphite with clay, the method still in use.

name: Wheelbarrow
desc: A wheelbarrow is a small hand-propelled vehicle, usually with one wheel, pushed and guided by a single person using two handles at the rear. The earliest evidence comes from Han dynasty China: a painted tomb mural at Chengdu in Sichuan, dated to 118 CE, shows a man pushing one. The Records of the Three Kingdoms credit the minister Zhuge Liang with a 'wooden ox' that carried military supplies in 231 CE. Chinese wheelbarrows mostly carried the load over a large central wheel, while those that appeared in medieval Europe between 1170 and 1250 had the wheel at or near the front.

name: Hot air balloon
desc: A hot air balloon is a lighter-than-air aircraft whose envelope holds heated air, with a basket or gondola for passengers and a source of heat hung beneath it. The French brothers Joseph-Michel and Jacques-Étienne Montgolfier developed one at Annonay in Ardèche and flew it unmanned in public in September 1783. On 21 November 1783 Jean-François Pilâtre de Rozier and François Laurent d'Arlandes made the first untethered manned flight, in Paris, in a Montgolfier balloon. The French used a balloon for observation at the battle of Fleurus in 1794, and Ed Yost and Jim Winker developed modern balloons with an onboard heat source from the 1950s.

name: Parachute
desc: A parachute is a device that slows an object's descent through an atmosphere by creating drag. The oldest known design appears in a manuscript of the 1470s attributed to Francesco di Giorgio Martini, a man hanging from a conical canopy, and Leonardo da Vinci sketched a pyramidal one about 1485. Louis-Sébastien Lenormand made the first recorded public jump, in France in 1783, and coined the word in 1785. André Garnerin made the first descent under a frameless silk canopy in 1797, Gleb Kotelnikov invented the knapsack parachute in 1911, and in World War I observers escaped from tethered balloons by parachute.

name: Helicopter
desc: A helicopter is a rotorcraft whose lift and thrust come from horizontally spinning rotors, so that it can take off and land vertically and hover. Chinese children played with bamboo flying toys from around 400 BCE, and Leonardo da Vinci designed an 'aerial screw' in the early 1480s. In 1907 the Breguet brothers' Gyroplane No. 1 lifted its pilot about 0.6 metres while men held it steady, and on 13 November 1907 Paul Cornu's machine made the first free flight with a pilot, in France. The Focke-Wulf Fw 61 of 1936 was the first practical helicopter, and Igor Sikorsky's R-4 of 1942 the first in full-scale production.

name: Junk
desc: A junk is a Chinese sailing ship with a central rudder, an overhanging flat transom, watertight bulkheads and a flat bottom, built with iron nails and clamps. It grew from tapering rafts rather than dugout canoes, and Chinese junks were at first river craft with square sails. Under the Song dynasty (960–1279) they took up ocean-going features from Southeast Asian ships: Zhu Yu's Pingzhou Table Talks, published by 1119, describes hulls divided by bulkheads, and the battened junk sail was adopted around the 12th century. Under the Yuan, Chinese trade ships displaced Southeast Asian ones on their Indian Ocean routes.

name: Dugout canoe
desc: A dugout canoe, or logboat, is a boat made from a hollowed-out tree, and the oldest boat type archaeologists have found. Before metal tools the log was hollowed with controlled fires and the burnt wood removed with an adze. The Pesse canoe from the Netherlands, carbon dated to between 8040 and 7510 BCE, is believed to be the world's oldest boat; the Dufuna canoe of Nigeria and a dugout from Kuahuqiao in Zhejiang, China, are both about 8,000 years old. Dugouts could be fitted with outriggers for rougher water, and they are still paddled and punted on lakes and rivers in Africa and Asia.

name: Horseshoe
desc: A horseshoe is a piece of equipment, usually nailed through the hoof wall, that protects a horse's hoof from wear. Its origin is uncertain, since worn iron was usually reforged: bronze shoes with apparent nail holes come from an Etruscan tomb of around 400 BCE, iron remnants from tombs in northeast China of the Goguryeo period dated to 414 CE, and a shoe with its nails from the tomb of the Frankish king Childeric I at Tournai. Written records of nailed shoes begin around 900 CE; by the Crusades horseshoes were widespread in Europe, and in China iron shoes became common under the Yuan dynasty.

name: Spear-thrower
desc: A spear-thrower, or atlatl, is a lever, usually about as long as the user's arm or forearm, with a cup or spur that holds the butt of a dart or javelin and throws it faster than the arm alone could. It is believed to have been used by Homo sapiens since the Upper Paleolithic, and the earliest known example is a Solutrean spear-thrower of reindeer antler, 17,500 years old, from Combe Saunière in the Dordogne, France. Ice Age hunters used it against megafauna; in Europe the bow and arrow supplemented it, while it stayed in use in the Americas, where Teotihuacan's warriors carried it, and in Australia as the woomera.

name: Bayonet
desc: A bayonet is a knife, dagger, sword or spike mounted on the barrel of a musket or rifle, so that the gun can be used as a spear in close combat. The first recorded bayonet proper is the 'gun-knife' of the son-and-mother gun in the Chinese military treatise Binglu of 1606, a plug bayonet pushed into the barrel. Jean Martinet standardized plug bayonets for new French fusilier regiments in 1671; because they stopped the gun from firing, socket bayonets that fitted around the barrel replaced them, and by the mid-18th century most European armies had adopted these for massed infantry charges.

name: Torpedo
desc: A torpedo is a self-propelled underwater weapon with an explosive warhead that detonates on contact with or close to its target. The word first named mines and spar torpedoes, used by Cornelius Drebbel, Robert Fulton and in the American Civil War. In 1864 the naval officer Giovanni Luppis gave the English engineer Robert Whitehead plans for a floating weapon at Fiume, now Rijeka in Croatia; Whitehead made from it the first modern self-propelled torpedo, run underwater by compressed air, and presented it to the Austrian Imperial Naval commission on 21 December 1866. On 16 January 1878 the Turkish steamer Intibah became the first ship sunk by self-propelled torpedoes.

name: Rifling
desc: Rifling is the helical grooving cut inside a gun barrel to spin the projectile, steadying its flight and making it more accurate. Its inventor is not known: straight 'soot grooves' were cut in small arms from at least 1480, and among the earliest recorded spiral-grooved barrels are those of the Vienna gunsmith Gaspard Kollner in 1498 and of Augustus Kotter of Nuremberg in 1520. Because the grooves had to be engraved by hand, rifled guns were at first used mostly by wealthy hunters, and they became common only in the mid-19th century; the first practical military rifled weapons were breech-loaders such as the Queen Anne pistol.

name: Crane
desc: A crane is a machine that lifts and moves loads with a boom, hoist, ropes or chains and sheaves, using levers and pulleys for mechanical advantage. The shaduf, a crane-like lever for lifting irrigation water, was used in ancient Mesopotamia and Egypt, but building cranes appear in Greece in the late 6th century BCE, attested by cuttings for lifting tongs and Lewis irons on temple blocks. The Romans added pulleys and treadwheels: a polyspastos worked by four men could lift 3,000 kg. Treadwheel cranes returned to Europe in the High Middle Ages for Gothic cathedrals and harbours, and steam engines, then internal combustion engines and electric motors, later powered them.

name: Typewriter
desc: The typewriter is a mechanical or electromechanical machine that prints characters on paper when a key is pressed, a type element striking an inked ribbon against the page. Its invention was incremental: Rasmus Malling-Hansen of Denmark invented the Hansen Writing Ball in 1865, and it went into commercial production in 1870 as the first typewriter sold. The first commercially successful model was patented in 1868 by Christopher Latham Sholes and others in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, and made by E. Remington and Sons from 1873 with the QWERTY layout, still the standard for English computer keyboards. Personal computers largely replaced typewriters after the 1980s.

name: Phonograph
desc: The phonograph is a device for the mechanical and analogue recording and reproduction of sound, in which a stylus traces a groove cut into a rotating cylinder or disc. Thomas Edison, working to play back recorded telegraph messages and to automate speech for the telephone, announced it in November 1877 and patented it in 1878; his first machines recorded on tinfoil wrapped round a grooved cylinder. Alexander Graham Bell's Volta Laboratory improved it in the 1880s with the graphophone and wax-coated cylinders, and in the 1890s Emile Berliner moved from cylinders to flat discs, naming his machine the gramophone. The disc record was the main commercial audio format for most of the 20th century.

name: Lithography
desc: Lithography is a planographic method of printing based on the immiscibility of oil and water: an image drawn with a greasy substance on smooth limestone or a metal plate takes the oily ink, while the wetted, etched surface around it repels it. The German author and actor Alois Senefelder invented it in the Electorate of Bavaria in 1796, and it was first used mostly for musical scores and maps. Godefroy Engelmann introduced multicolour printing, chromolithography, in 1837, and offset lithography, in which a rubber cylinder carries the ink from plate to paper, has printed most books and magazines since the 1960s.

name: Morse code
desc: Morse code is a method of telecommunication that encodes letters, numerals and punctuation as standard sequences of two signal durations, dots and dashes. Around 1837 the American artist Samuel Morse devised a code of numerals for the electrical telegraph he was developing with Joseph Henry and Alfred Vail; in 1840 Vail extended it to letters, giving the shortest signs to the commonest ones, and this code was first used in 1844. Friedrich Gerke's simpler Hamburg alphabet of 1848, adopted in Germany and Austria in 1851, led to the International Morse code of 1865, which also carried early radio communication from the 1890s.

name: Braille
desc: Braille is a tactile writing system used by blind and visually impaired people, in which characters are formed by six raised dots arranged in two columns of three, the braille cell. Louis Braille, a Frenchman who had lost his sight in a childhood accident, developed it in 1824 at the age of fifteen as an improvement on Charles Barbier's night writing, whose sets of 12 embossed dots encoded 36 sounds; Braille's cells stood for the letters of the French alphabet and added numerals and punctuation. He published the system, with musical notation, in 1829. Braille codes now exist for over 133 languages.

name: Radar
desc: Radar is a system that uses radio waves to find the distance, direction and speed of objects such as aircraft, ships and weather formations; the United States Navy coined the name in 1940 from radio detection and ranging. In 1904 the German inventor Christian Hülsmeyer detected a ship in dense fog with his telemobiloscope, but German military officials rejected it. Pulsed radar was first shown in December 1934 by Robert M. Page at the Naval Research Laboratory, and in Britain Robert Watson-Watt's team built the Chain Home stations, operational from 1936, which helped the Royal Air Force win the Battle of Britain. The cavity magnetron made small sets possible.

name: Personal computer
desc: A personal computer is a computer designed to be operated directly by one user, rather than shared by many through time-sharing like a minicomputer or mainframe. It was made possible by the integrated circuit and the microprocessor, the first single-chip one being the Intel 4004 of 1971; the Micral N, built from 1972, was the earliest commercial, non-kit microcomputer based on a microprocessor. The Altair 8800 of 1974 was the first commercially successful personal computer, the Commodore PET, Apple II and TRS-80 brought ready-assembled machines to a mass market in 1977, and the IBM Personal Computer of 1981 set the standard its compatibles followed.

name: Email
desc: Email, or electronic mail, is a method of sending and receiving digital messages over a computer network, on a store-and-forward model in which servers accept, forward, deliver and store messages. Messaging between users of the same computer became possible with time-sharing in the early 1960s, with a notable implementation in MIT's CTSS project in 1965. In 1971 the first network mail was sent over the ARPANET, introducing addresses with the @ symbol for the user's system; the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol was implemented on the ARPANET in 1983, and after 1995 SMTP, POP3 and IMAP became the standard.

name: Transatlantic telegraph cable
desc: The transatlantic telegraph cables were undersea cables laid across the Atlantic Ocean for telegraph communication between Europe and the Americas. The Atlantic Telegraph Company, led by Cyrus West Field, laid the first from Valentia Island off Ireland to Trinity Bay, Newfoundland, and it carried its first messages on August 16, 1858, among them Queen Victoria's congratulations to President James Buchanan, but it failed after three weeks. Cables laid from the SS Great Eastern in 1865 and 1866 proved durable, and since 1866 the continents have been linked, so that a message could be answered on the same day rather than after weeks by ship.

name: Mercator projection
desc: The Mercator projection is a way of drawing the globe on a flat map in which courses of constant compass bearing, rhumb lines, appear as straight lines, so that a chart serves sailors directly. Gerardus Mercator introduced it on his world map of 1569, printed from 18 copper plates he engraved himself, by increasing the degrees of latitude towards each pole as the parallels lengthen. He left no account of his method, and Edward Wright and others later showed how to calculate the latitude scale exactly. Acceptance was slow and came only with the French sea atlas Le Neptune Francois at the end of the seventeenth century; the projection is still the basis of navigation charts.

name: Library of Ashurbanipal
desc: The Library of Ashurbanipal is a collection of more than 30,000 clay tablets and fragments of the 7th century BCE, gathered at Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, by Ashurbanipal, king of the Neo-Assyrian Empire from 668 to 627 BCE. He had cities and centres of learning across Mesopotamia send him copies of their texts, sent scribes to collect them and took tablets as war loot; the texts, mostly Akkadian in cuneiform, were placed in rooms by subject and marked with coloured signs or their first words. The fire that destroyed Nineveh in 612 BCE baked the tablets, among them the Epic of Gilgamesh. Most are now in the British Museum.

name: Fired brick
desc: Fired brick is brick of clay and shale baked in a kiln, harder and longer-lasting than the older sun-dried mudbrick. Mesopotamia had discovered it between 5000 and 4500 BCE, and the earliest fired bricks of China appeared around 4400 BCE at Chengtoushan, a walled settlement of the Daxi culture, where they paved house floors. Indus Valley cities such as Kalibangan used it by 3000 BCE, and the Roman legions stamped the bricks of their mobile kilns across the empire. The first brick-making machine was patented in 1852, as the Industrial Revolution multiplied production.

name: Flying buttress
desc: A flying buttress is a ramping arch that carries the outward thrust of a stone vault or roof from the upper part of a wall across open space to a massive pier standing away from it. Ancient examples survive on the Basilica of San Vitale in Ravenna and the Rotunda of Galerius in Thessaloniki, and Romanesque churches such as Durham Cathedral hid similar arches under their gallery roofs. By the 1160s builders in the Île-de-France ran longer, visible arches over the aisles, as at Saint-Germain-des-Prés, completed in 1163, and Notre Dame de Paris in 1180. Walls could then be thinner, with larger windows of stained glass, and the flying buttress became a defining feature of Gothic architecture.

name: Reinforced concrete
desc: Reinforced concrete is concrete with embedded iron or steel bars or mesh, which take the tension plain concrete cannot bear while the concrete resists compression. It was developed in parallel in England and France in the mid-19th century. The French builder François Coignet built the first iron-reinforced concrete structure, a four-story house in the suburbs of Paris, in 1853–55, and in 1854 the English builder William B. Wilkinson reinforced the roof and floors of a house with knowledge of tensile stresses. Joseph Monier patented reinforced flowerpots in 1867 and columns and girders in 1877, and the firm Wayss & Freytag made the first commercial use of it in 1884.

name: Portland cement
desc: Portland cement is a hydraulic cement made by heating limestone and clay minerals in a kiln to form clinker, then grinding it with a little gypsum; it is the most common cement and the basic ingredient of concrete and mortar. Joseph Aspdin patented it in England in 1824 and named it after Portland stone, quarried on the Isle of Portland in Dorset. It grew out of the natural cements made in Britain from the middle of the 18th century, John Smeaton’s experiments of 1756 and Louis Vicat’s artificial hydraulic lime. His son William Aspdin improved it in the 1840s at Rotherhithe, and the rotary kiln, patented in 1885, allowed continuous manufacture.

name: Hypocaust
desc: A hypocaust is a system of central heating in which hot air and smoke from a furnace circulate beneath a floor raised on stacks of tiles, the pilae, and rise through clay or tile flues in the walls. Vitruvius attributes its invention to Sergius Orata around 80 BCE, and described its construction in his De architectura of about 15 BCE. Hypocausts heated public baths and the villas of the wealthy throughout the Roman Empire, and their remains survive across Europe, western Asia and northern Africa. The system fell out of use in the western provinces as the empire declined, but lived on in the Eastern Roman Empire and in the baths of Al Andalus.

name: Vulcanization
desc: Vulcanization is the hardening of rubber, originally of natural rubber treated with sulfur and heat, which forms cross-links between its polymer chains and makes it firmer and more durable. Ancient Mesoamerican cultures already cured rubber with sulfur-rich plant juices, an early form of the process. Charles Goodyear, who worked in the 1830s to strengthen rubber, found in 1839 that a mixture of rubber and sulfur dropped on a hot pan hardened instead of melting, and by 1844 he had patented the process and produced the rubber on an industrial scale. Thomas Hancock had taken out a British patent eight weeks earlier, in November 1843.

name: Friction match
desc: A friction match is a small stick tipped with a mixture that ignites when struck against a rough surface. Pinewood sticks tipped with sulfur, lit from a flame, are described in China around 950, and in 1805 Jean Chancel of Paris made a match lit by dipping it in sulfuric acid. The first commercially successful friction match was made by John Walker, a chemist and pharmacist of Stockton-on-Tees, England, and first recorded in April 1827: sticks tipped with antimony trisulfide and potassium chlorate. Samuel Jones sold an improved version as the lucifer, and Gustaf Erik Pasch’s striking surface of red phosphorus of 1844 led to the safety match.

name: Egyptian blue
desc: Egyptian blue, a calcium copper silicate, is a pigment made by heating silica, lime, a copper compound and an alkali, and is considered the first synthetic pigment. The earliest evidence of its use is on an alabaster bowl of the late pre-dynastic period, Naqada III, about 3250 BCE, excavated at Hierakonpolis. Egyptians made it to imitate turquoise and lapis lazuli and painted it on tombs, wall paintings, furnishings and statues; it is also found in the Near East, the Eastern Mediterranean and the Roman Empire. Vitruvius described how it was made in the first century BCE, but its use died out in the fourth century CE and the method was forgotten until modern analysis.

name: Lacquerware
desc: Lacquerware consists of objects coated with lacquer, in East Asia an urushiol-based lacquer from the dried sap of the lacquer tree, Toxicodendron vernicifluum. The oldest known lacquerware, burial ornaments from an Initial Jōmon pit grave at the Kakinoshima site in Hakodate, Hokkaido, Japan, is about 9,000 years old, and the earliest in China is a red wooden bowl from a Hemudu culture site in Zhejiang. Chinese lacquer became a decorative art under the Shang dynasty and a commercial industry in the state of Chu under the Eastern Zhou, and spread to Korea and Japan; the traditions of Southeast Asia, South Asia and the Americas arose independently.

name: Sulfuric acid
desc: Sulfuric acid, called oil of vitriol by medieval alchemists, is a strong acid first made by distilling vitriols, the hydrated sulfates of metals. The Jabirian authors and Abu Bakr al-Razi distilled vitriols, and al-Razi may have made the acid unknowingly; according to Ahmad Y. al-Hassan, an anonymous Garshuni manuscript from before c. 1100 holds three recipes for it. European works first allude to it in the thirteenth century. Joshua Ward of London began large-scale production in 1736, John Roebuck’s lead chamber process of 1746 in Birmingham industrialised it, and Peregrine Phillips patented the contact process in 1831, by which nearly all of it is made today.

name: Electrolysis
desc: Electrolysis is the use of a direct electric current to drive a chemical reaction that would not otherwise occur, as in separating elements from ores and compounds. In 1800 William Nicholson and Anthony Carlisle, furthering Volta’s experiments, placed the wires of a voltaic pile in water and saw hydrogen and oxygen bubble from them. Humphry Davy discovered potassium, sodium, barium, calcium and magnesium by electrolysis by 1808, and his assistant Michael Faraday published two laws of electrolysis and introduced the word in 1834. The method later yielded gallium in 1875, fluorine in 1886 and, through the Hall–Héroult process of the same year, aluminium.

name: Hall–Héroult process
desc: The Hall–Héroult process is the major industrial process for smelting aluminium: alumina, obtained most often from bauxite, is dissolved in molten cryolite and the bath is electrolysed at 940–980 °C, giving metal of 99.5–99.8% purity. It was discovered independently and almost simultaneously in 1886 by the American chemist Charles Martin Hall and the Frenchman Paul Héroult, both 22 years old. Before it, aluminium was made with sodium or potassium and cost more than gold; Hall opened the first large-scale plant in Pittsburgh in 1888, later Alcoa, and with cheaper electric power the metal became an inexpensive commodity. The process uses much electricity and can emit much carbon dioxide.

name: Stethoscope
desc: The stethoscope is a medical device for listening to the sounds of the heart, lungs and intestines and to blood flow, a practice called auscultation. René Laennec invented it in 1816 at the Necker-Enfants Malades Hospital in Paris: a monaural wooden tube, devised after he found that a rolled piece of paper carried heart sounds without his ear touching the patient's chest. Golding Bird described one with a flexible tube in 1840, and Arthur Leared made a binaural stethoscope in 1851. George Philip Cammann's design of the following year, with a plug for each ear, has remained essentially unchanged since.

name: Blood transfusion
desc: Blood transfusion is the transfer of blood or its components into the veins of a human or other animal. The physician Richard Lower performed the first reliably documented successful transfusion, between two dogs, in February 1665, and described it to the Royal Society that December. On 15 June 1667 Jean-Baptiste Denys transfused a sheep's blood into a 15-year-old boy, but deaths after such experiments led to bans in 1668. James Blundell performed the first successful transfusion of human blood, for bleeding after childbirth, in 1818 at Guy's Hospital in London, and Karl Landsteiner's discovery of blood groups in 1901 gave the practice a scientific basis.

name: Prosthesis
desc: A prosthesis is an artificial device that replaces a missing body part lost through injury, disease or a condition present at birth. The earliest archaeological evidence is an eye prosthesis, probably of bitumen paste covered with a thin layer of gold, buried with a woman at Shahr-i Shōkhta in Iran about 3000 to 2800 BCE. A wood and leather artificial big toe found on a mummy near Thebes, dated 950 to 710 BCE, shows signs of use. Ambroise Paré, considered the father of modern prosthetics, designed an above-knee device, and functional prostheses appeared in the 1500s.

name: Sulfonamide
desc: Sulfonamides, or sulfa drugs, were the first broadly effective antibacterial medicines used systemically. Experiments began in 1932 in the laboratories of Bayer AG, then part of IG Farben, where a team led by Gerhard Domagk found that Prontosil, a red dye synthesised by Josef Klarer, stopped some bacterial infections in mice; the first report appeared in 1935. A team at the Pasteur Institute showed that the body breaks Prontosil down into sulfanilamide, a compound first made in 1906 whose patent had expired. Between 1937 and 1943 sulfa drugs lowered maternal mortality in the United States by 25–40%.

name: Artificial cardiac pacemaker
desc: An artificial cardiac pacemaker is a medical device that sends electrical pulses through electrodes to the chambers of the heart to keep an even heart rate. The first fully implantable pacemaker, designed by the inventor Rune Elmqvist and the surgeon Åke Senning, was implanted on 8 October 1958 at the Karolinska Institute in Solna, Sweden; it failed after three hours, and its patient, Arne Larsson, went on to receive 26 pacemakers. Earlier devices were external, from Mark C Lidwill's apparatus of 1926 in Sydney to John Hopps's of 1950. Wilson Greatbatch's lithium iodide cell of 1971 led to pacemakers lasting up to eleven years.

name: Organ transplantation
desc: Organ transplantation is the removal of an organ or tissue from one body and its placement in another, to replace a damaged or missing function. The first transplant in the modern sense was performed in 1883 by the Swiss surgeon Theodor Kocher, who reversed the symptoms that followed the complete removal of the thyroid by implanting thyroid tissue. Alexis Carrel's techniques for joining blood vessels, from the early 1900s, laid the groundwork for later transplant surgery, but rejection defeated most attempts until Joseph Murray's kidney transplant between identical twins in Boston in 1954. Christiaan Barnard performed the first human-to-human heart transplant in 1967.

name: Electric motor
desc: An electric motor is a machine that converts electrical energy into mechanical energy, usually through the interaction of a magnetic field and the current in a wire winding. Michael Faraday first showed electromagnetic rotation on 3 September 1821 at the Royal Institution, where a wire carrying a current turned around a magnet in a pool of mercury. Ányos Jedlik built a device with a stator, rotor and commutator in 1828, William Sturgeon a DC motor able to turn machinery in 1832, and Frank Julian Sprague the first practical DC motor in 1886. Galileo Ferraris and Nikola Tesla invented AC induction motors in 1885 and 1887.

name: Diesel engine
desc: A diesel engine is an internal combustion engine in which the fuel is ignited by the heat of air compressed in the cylinder, without a spark plug. The German engineer Rudolf Diesel published his idea in 1893 in Theory and Construction of a Rational Heat Motor, and his first prototype was built that summer at the Maschinenfabrik Augsburg, with the first ignition on 10 August 1893. A redesigned engine ran for 88 revolutions in February 1894, and the third prototype, tested on 17 February 1897, reached an effective efficiency of 26.2%, against the 6–10% of steam engines that Diesel had learned of as a student.

name: Hydroelectricity
desc: Hydroelectricity is electricity generated from hydropower, the energy of moving water. Water had long driven machinery, but the first hydroelectric power scheme was developed in 1878 by William Armstrong at Cragside in Northumberland, England, where it powered a single arc lamp in his art gallery. The Schoelkopf Power Station No. 1 near Niagara Falls began to produce electricity in 1881, and by 1889 there were 200 hydroelectric power stations in the United States alone. Dams grew larger through the 20th century, to the Three Gorges Dam in China at 22.5 GW, and hydropower supplied 15% of the world's electricity in 2023.

name: Alternating current
desc: Alternating current is an electric current that periodically reverses direction, the form in which electric power is delivered to homes and businesses. The French instrument maker Hippolyte Pixii built the first alternator to produce it in 1832, on Michael Faraday's principles. In 1885 Károly Zipernowsky, Ottó Bláthy and Miksa Déri of the Ganz Works in Budapest patented closed-core transformers, and their system of 75 transformers supplied 1,067 lamps at the Hungarian National Exhibition that May. Westinghouse then built AC systems across the United States, and the first three-phase system was established in Frankfurt in 1891.

name: Lithium-ion battery
desc: A lithium-ion battery is a rechargeable battery that stores energy by moving lithium ions in and out of electronically conducting solids. M. Stanley Whittingham conceived intercalation electrodes in the 1970s and made the first rechargeable lithium-ion battery, with a titanium disulfide cathode, though safety problems kept it from being commercialized. John Goodenough used lithium cobalt oxide as a cathode in 1980, and Akira Yoshino developed the first prototype of the modern battery, with a carbonaceous anode, in 1985. A Sony and Asahi Kasei team led by Yoshio Nishi brought it to market in 1991, and the three inventors shared the 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

name: Wind turbine
desc: A wind turbine is a device that converts the kinetic energy of wind into electrical energy. The first to generate electricity was installed by the Austrian Josef Friedländer at the Vienna International Electrical Exhibition in 1883: a Halladay wind motor 6.6 m across, whose 3.7 kW drove a dynamo that charged batteries. James Blyth lit his holiday home in Marykirk, Scotland, with one in July 1887, and Charles F. Brush built the first automatically operated wind turbine some months later. A 100 kW forerunner of modern horizontal-axis machines ran at Yalta in 1931, and by 2024 turbines generated over 1,136 gigawatts.
